claim: HIV-1 integrase (IN) alterations referred to as class II substitutions exhibit pleiotropic effects during virus replication.
source: A large number of human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) integrase (IN) alterations, referred to as class II substitutions, exhibit pleiotropic effects during virus replication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about class II IN substitutions.

claim: All tested class II IN substitutions compromised IN-RNA binding in virions.
source: Here we demonstrate that all tested class II IN substitutions compromised IN-RNA binding in virions by one of the three distinct mechanisms
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Class II IN substitutions can compromise IN-RNA binding by markedly reducing IN levels thus precluding the formation of IN complexes with viral RNA.
source: all tested class II IN substitutions compromised IN-RNA binding in virions by one of the three distinct mechanisms: (i) markedly reducing IN levels thus precluding the formation of IN complexes with viral RNA
evidence: This is one of three mechanisms identified through experimental data in the study.

claim: Class II IN substitutions can compromise IN-RNA binding by adversely affecting functional IN multimerization and consequently impairing IN binding to viral RNA.
source: all tested class II IN substitutions compromised IN-RNA binding in virions by one of the three distinct mechanisms: (i) markedly reducing IN levels thus precluding the formation of IN complexes with viral RNA; (ii) adversely affecting functional IN multimerization and consequently impairing IN binding to viral RNA
evidence: This is the second mechanism identified through experimental data in the study.

claim: Class II IN substitutions can compromise IN-RNA binding by directly compromising IN-RNA interactions without substantially affecting IN levels or functional IN multimerization.
source: all tested class II IN substitutions compromised IN-RNA binding in virions by one of the three distinct mechanisms: (i) markedly reducing IN levels thus precluding the formation of IN complexes with viral RNA; (ii) adversely affecting functional IN multimerization and consequently impairing IN binding to viral RNA; and (iii) directly compromising IN-RNA interactions without substantially affecting IN levels or functional IN multimerization.
evidence: This is the third mechanism identified through experimental data in the study.

claim: Inhibition of IN-RNA interactions resulted in the mislocalization of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes outside the capsid lattice.
source: Inhibition of IN-RNA interactions resulted in the mislocalization of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes outside the capsid lattice, which led to premature degradation of the viral genome and IN in target cells.
evidence: This is a finding demonstrated through experimental data in the study.

claim: Mislocalization of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes outside the capsid lattice led to premature degradation of the viral genome in target cells.
source: Inhibition of IN-RNA interactions resulted in the mislocalization of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes outside the capsid lattice, which led to premature degradation of the viral genome and IN in target cells.
evidence: This is a finding demonstrated through experimental data in the study.

claim: Mislocalization of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes outside the capsid lattice led to premature degradation of IN in target cells.
source: Inhibition of IN-RNA interactions resulted in the mislocalization of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes outside the capsid lattice, which led to premature degradation of the viral genome and IN in target cells.
evidence: This is a finding demonstrated through experimental data in the study.

claim: IN-RNA interactions play an essential role in accurate virion maturation.
source: Collectively, our studies uncover causal mechanisms for the class II phenotype and highlight an essential role of IN-RNA interactions for accurate virion maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: At the plasma membrane of an infected cell, Gag and Gag-Pol molecules assemble around a vRNA dimer and bud from the cell as a spherical immature virion.
source: At the plasma membrane of an infected cell, Gag and Gag-Pol molecules assemble around a vRNA dimer and bud from the cell as a spherical immature virion, in which the Gag proteins are radially arranged (Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012; Pornillos and Ganser-Pornillos, 2019; Bieniasz and Telesnitsky, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In immature virions, Gag proteins are radially arranged.
source: At the plasma membrane of an infected cell, Gag and Gag-Pol molecules assemble around a vRNA dimer and bud from the cell as a spherical immature virion, in which the Gag proteins are radially arranged (Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012; Pornillos and Ganser-Pornillos, 2019; Bieniasz and Telesnitsky, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: As the immature virion buds, the viral protease enzyme is activated and cleaves Gag and Gag-Pol into their constituent domains, triggering virion maturation.
source: As the immature virion buds, the viral protease enzyme is activated and cleaves Gag and Gag-Pol into their constituent domains, triggering virion maturation (Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012; Pornillos and Ganser-Pornillos, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During maturation, the cleaved nucleocapsid (NC) domain of Gag condenses with the RNA genome and pol-encoded viral enzymes inside the conical capsid lattice.
source: During maturation, the cleaved nucleocapsid (NC) domain of Gag condenses with the RNA genome and pol-encoded viral enzymes (reverse transcriptase [RT] and integrase [IN]) inside the conical capsid lattice, composed of the cleaved capsid (CA) protein, which together forms the core (Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012; Pornillos and Ganser-Pornillos, 2019; Bieniasz and Telesnitsky, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The conical capsid lattice is composed of the cleaved capsid (CA) protein.
source: During maturation, the cleaved nucleocapsid (NC) domain of Gag condenses with the RNA genome and pol-encoded viral enzymes (reverse transcriptase [RT] and integrase [IN]) inside the conical capsid lattice, composed of the cleaved capsid (CA) protein, which together forms the core (Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012; Pornillos and Ganser-Pornillos, 2019; Bieniasz and Telesnitsky, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: After infection of a target cell, RT in the confines of the reverse transcription complex (RTC) synthesizes linear double-stranded DNA from vRNA.
source: After infection of a target cell, RT in the confines of the reverse transcription complex (RTC) synthesizes linear double-stranded DNA from vRNA (Engelman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The vDNA is subsequently imported into the nucleus, where the IN enzyme catalyzes its insertion into the host cell chromosome.
source: The vDNA is subsequently imported into the nucleus, where the IN enzyme catalyzes its insertion into the host cell chromosome (Engelman, 2019; Lesbats et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Integration is mediated by the intasome nucleoprotein complex that consists of a multimer of IN engaging both ends of linear vDNA.
source: Integration is mediated by the intasome nucleoprotein complex that consists of a multimer of IN engaging both ends of linear vDNA (Engelman and Cherepanov, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The number of IN protomers required for intasome function varies across Retroviridae.
source: While the number of IN protomers required for intasome function varies across Retroviridae, single-particle cryogenic electron microscopic (cryo-EM) structures of HIV-1 and Maedi-visna virus indicate that lentivirus integration proceeds via respective higher-order dodecamer and hexadecamer IN arrangements (Ballandras-Colas et al., 2017; Passos et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Single-particle cryo-EM structures of HIV-1 indicate that lentivirus integration proceeds via higher-order dodecamer IN arrangements.
source: While the number of IN protomers required for intasome function varies across Retroviridae, single-particle cryogenic electron microscopic (cryo-EM) structures of HIV-1 and Maedi-visna virus indicate that lentivirus integration proceeds via respective higher-order dodecamer and hexadecamer IN arrangements (Ballandras-Colas et al., 2017; Passos et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Single-particle cryo-EM structures of Maedi-visna virus indicate that lentivirus integration proceeds via hexadecamer IN arrangements.
source: While the number of IN protomers required for intasome function varies across Retroviridae, single-particle cryogenic electron microscopic (cryo-EM) structures of HIV-1 and Maedi-visna virus indicate that lentivirus integration proceeds via respective higher-order dodecamer and hexadecamer IN arrangements (Ballandras-Colas et al., 2017; Passos et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A lower-order intasome composed of an HIV-1 IN tetramer was resolvable by cryo-EM.
source: though a lower-order intasome composed of an HIV-1 IN tetramer was also resolvable by cryo-EM (Passos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A number of IN substitutions which specifically arrest HIV-1 replication at the integration step have been described and are grouped into class I.
source: A number of IN substitutions which specifically arrest HIV-1 replication at the integration step have been described (Engelman, 1999). These substitutions are grouped into class I to delineate them from a variety of other IN substitutions, which exhibit pleiotropic effects, and are collectively referred to as class II substitutions (Engelman, 1999; Engelman et al., 1995; Engelman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Class II IN substitutions or deletions of entire IN impair proper particle assembly.
source: Class II IN substitutions or deletions of entire IN impair proper particle assembly (Engelman et al., 1995; Ansari-Lari et al., 1995; Bukovsky and Göttlinger, 1996; Jenkins et al., 1996; Kalpana et al., 1999; Leavitt et al., 1996; Liao and Wang, 2004; Lu et al., 2005a; Lu et al., 2004; Nakamura et al., 1997; Quillent et al., 1996; Shin et al., 1994; Taddeo et al., 1994; Wu et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Class II IN substitutions or deletions of entire IN impair morphogenesis.
source: morphogenesis (Engelman et al., 1995; Jenkins et al., 1996; Nakamura et al., 1997; Quillent et al., 1996; Shin et al., 1994; Fontana et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2013; Kessl et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Class II IN substitutions or deletions of entire IN impair reverse transcription in target cells.
source: and reverse transcription in target cells (Engelman, 1999; Engelman et al., 1995; Leavitt et al., 1996; Lu et al., 2005a; Lu et al., 2004; Nakamura et al., 1997; Shin et al., 1994; Wu et al., 1999; Fontana et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2013; Kessl et al., 2016; Ao et al., 2005; Busschots et al., 2007; Engelman et al., 1997; Limón et al., 2002; Lloyd et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2005b; Masuda et al., 1995; Rahman et al., 2007; Rivière et al., 2010; Tsurutani et al., 2000; Wiskerchen and Muesing, 1995; Zhu et al., 2004; De Houwer et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2013; Mohammed et al., 2011; Shehu-Xhilaga et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some class II IN substitutions impair reverse transcription in target cells without impacting IN catalytic function in vitro.
source: in some cases without impacting IN catalytic function in vitro (Jenkins et al., 1996; Kalpana et al., 1999; Lu et al., 2005a; Lu et al., 2004; Busschots et al., 2007; Engelman et al., 1997; Lu et al., 2005b; Rahman et al., 2007; Engelman and Craigie, 1992; Lutzke and Plasterk, 1998; Lutzke et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A hallmark morphological defect of class II IN mutant viruses is the formation of aberrant viral particles with viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) complexes mislocalized outside the conical CA lattice.
source: A hallmark morphological defect of these viruses is the formation of aberrant viral particles with viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) complexes mislocalized outside the conical CA lattice (Engelman et al., 1995; Jenkins et al., 1996; Nakamura et al., 1997; Quillent et al., 1996; Shin et al., 1994; Fontana et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2013; Kessl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strikingly similar morphological defects are observed in virions produced from cells treated with allosteric integrase inhibitors (ALLINIs).
source: Strikingly similar morphological defects are observed in virions produced from cells treated with allosteric integrase inhibitors (ALLINIs, also known as LEDGINs, NCINIs, INLAIs, or MINIs; Fontana et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2013; Balakrishnan et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2014; Le Rouzic et al., 2013; Desimmie et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2014; Amadori et al., 2017; Gupta et al., 2014; Bonnard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ALLINIs induce aberrant IN multimerization in virions by engaging the V-shaped pocket at the IN dimer interface.
source: ALLINIs induce aberrant IN multimerization in virions by engaging the V-shaped pocket at the IN dimer interface, which also provides a principal binding site for the host integration targeting cofactor lens epithelium-derived growth factor (LEDGF)/p75 (Le Rouzic et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2016; Koneru et al., 2019; Kessl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The V-shaped pocket at the IN dimer interface provides a principal binding site for the host integration targeting cofactor LEDGF/p75.
source: ALLINIs induce aberrant IN multimerization in virions by engaging the V-shaped pocket at the IN dimer interface, which also provides a principal binding site for the host integration targeting cofactor lens epithelium-derived growth factor (LEDGF)/p75 (Le Rouzic et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2016; Koneru et al., 2019; Kessl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HIV-1 IN binds to the vRNA genome in virions.
source: The recent discovery that HIV-1 IN binds to the vRNA genome in virions and that inhibiting IN-RNA interactions leads to the formation of eccentric particles provided initial clues about the role of IN during virion morphogenesis (Kessl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Inhibiting IN-RNA interactions leads to the formation of eccentric particles.
source: The recent discovery that HIV-1 IN binds to the vRNA genome in virions and that inhibiting IN-RNA interactions leads to the formation of eccentric particles provided initial clues about the role of IN during virion morphogenesis (Kessl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HIV-1 IN consists of three independently folded protein domains: the N-terminal domain (NTD), catalytic core domain (CCD), and C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: HIV-1 IN consists of three independently folded protein domains: the N-terminal domain (NTD), catalytic core domain (CCD), and C-terminal domain (CTD) (Engelman and Cherepanov, 2017; Engelman and Cherepanov, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: vRNA binding is mediated by a constellation of basic residues within the CTD.
source: and vRNA binding is mediated by a constellation of basic residues within the CTD (Kessl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Aberrant IN multimerization underlies the inhibition of IN-RNA interactions by ALLINIs.
source: Notably, aberrant IN multimerization underlies the inhibition of IN-RNA interactions by ALLINIs (Kessl et al., 2016) and subsequent defects in virion maturation (Fontana et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2013; Kessl et al., 2016; Balakrishnan et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2014; Desimmie et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2014; Amadori et al., 2017; Gupta et al., 2014; Bonnard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Eccentric virions generated via class II IN substitutions or ALLINI treatment are defective for reverse transcription in target cells.
source: Eccentric virions generated via class II IN substitutions or ALLINI treatment are defective for reverse transcription in target cells (Engelman, 1999; Engelman et al., 1995; Leavitt et al., 1996; Lu et al., 2005a; Lu et al., 2004; Nakamura et al., 1997; Shin et al., 1994; Wu et al., 1999; Fontana et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2013; Kessl et al., 2016; Ao et al., 2005; Busschots et al., 2007; Engelman et al., 1997; Limón et al., 2002; Lloyd et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2005b; Masuda et al., 1995; Rahman et al., 2007; Rivière et al., 2010; Tsurutani et al., 2000; Wiskerchen and Muesing, 1995; Zhu et al., 2004; De Houwer et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2013; Mohammed et al., 2011; Shehu-Xhilaga et al., 2002; Balakrishnan et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2014; Desimmie et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2014; Gupta et al., 2016; Tekeste et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Eccentric virions contain equivalent levels of RT and vRNA genome as wild type particles.
source: despite containing equivalent levels of RT and vRNA genome as wild type (WT) particles (Fontana et al., 2015; van Bel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neither the condensation of the viral genome by NC nor its priming appears to be affected in eccentric virions.
source: In addition, neither the condensation of the viral genome by NC (Fontana et al., 2015; van Bel et al., 2014) nor its priming (van Bel et al., 2014) appears to be affected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Premature loss of the viral genome and IN, as well as spatial separation of RT from vRNPs, may underlie the reverse transcription defect observed in eccentric viruses generated in the presence of ALLINIs or the class II IN R269A/K273A substitutions.
source: We and others have recently shown that premature loss of the viral genome and IN, as well as spatial separation of RT from vRNPs, may underlie the reverse transcription defect observed in eccentric viruses generated in the presence of ALLINIs or the class II IN R269A/K273A substitutions (Koneru et al., 2019; Madison et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The capsid lattice or IN binding to vRNA itself is necessary to protect viral components from the host environment upon entering a target cell.
source: These findings support a model in which the capsid lattice or IN binding to vRNA itself is necessary to protect viral components from the host environment upon entering a target cell.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on previous findings cited in the text.

claim: Substitutions in IN had no measurable effect on Gag (Pr55) expression.
source: While substitutions in IN had no measurable effect on Gag (Pr55) expression, modest effects on Gag processing in cells was visible for several missense mutant viruses including H12N, N18I, K34A, Y99A, K103E, W108R, F185K, Q214L/Q216L, L242A, V260E, as well as the ΔIN mutant (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Modest effects on Gag processing in cells was visible for several missense mutant viruses including H12N, N18I, K34A, Y99A, K103E, W108R, F185K, Q214L/Q216L, L242A, V260E, as well as the ΔIN mutant.
source: While substitutions in IN had no measurable effect on Gag (Pr55) expression, modest effects on Gag processing in cells was visible for several missense mutant viruses including H12N, N18I, K34A, Y99A, K103E, W108R, F185K, Q214L/Q216L, L242A, V260E, as well as the ΔIN mutant (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Particle release was largely similar between WT and IN mutant viruses, as evident by the similar levels of CA protein present in cell culture supernatants.
source: Nevertheless, particle release was largely similar between WT and IN mutant viruses, as evident by the similar levels of CA protein present in cell culture supernatants (Figure 2A, lower panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Virion-associated IN was at least 5-fold less than WT with several mutants, including H12N, N18I, K103E, W108R, F185K, L242A, and V260E.
source: First, virion-associated IN was at least 5-fold less than WT with several mutants, including H12N, N18I, K103E, W108R, F185K, L242A, and V260E (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: IN substitutions H12N, N18I, K103E, W108R, F185K, L242A, and V260E reduced levels of Gag-Pol processing intermediates in producer cells.
source: Notably, these substitutions also reduced levels of Gag-Pol processing intermediates in producer cells (Figure 2A) and RT in virions (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that they likely destabilized the Gag-Pol precursor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IN substitutions H12N, N18I, K103E, W108R, F185K, L242A, and V260E likely destabilized the Gag-Pol precursor.
source: Notably, these substitutions also reduced levels of Gag-Pol processing intermediates in producer cells (Figure 2A) and RT in virions (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that they likely destabilized the Gag-Pol precursor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these substitutions reduced Gag-Pol processing intermediates and RT in virions.

claim: The R228A substitution abolished full-length IN in virions without impacting cell- or virion-associated Gag-Pol levels or processing intermediates.
source: Second, the R228A substitution abolished full-length IN in virions without impacting cell- or virion-associated Gag-Pol levels or processing intermediates; however, a faster migrating species generated by aberrant IN processing and/or IN degradation was visible.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claim: A faster migrating species generated by aberrant IN processing and/or IN degradation was visible with the R228A substitution.
source: Second, the R228A substitution abolished full-length IN in virions without impacting cell- or virion-associated Gag-Pol levels or processing intermediates; however, a faster migrating species generated by aberrant IN processing and/or IN degradation was visible.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claim: The K34A mutant was incorporated into virions at a modestly reduced level alongside a smaller protein species.
source: A similar but more modest defect was observed for the K34A mutant, which was incorporated into virions at a modestly reduced level alongside a smaller protein species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data.

claim: With the exception of E96A, nearly all of the IN substitutions reduced virus titers at least 100-fold compared to the WT.
source: With the exception of E96A, nearly all of the IN substitutions reduced virus titers at least 100-fold compared to the WT (Figure 2B), which corresponded with reduced levels of reverse-transcription in infected cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Reduced virus titers corresponded with reduced levels of reverse-transcription in infected cells.
source: With the exception of E96A, nearly all of the IN substitutions reduced virus titers at least 100-fold compared to the WT (Figure 2B), which corresponded with reduced levels of reverse-transcription in infected cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Class II mutant IN molecules had variable levels of catalytic activity as assessed by the ability of Vpr-IN proteins to transcomplement a catalytically inactive IN (D116N).
source: In line with previous reports (Lu et al., 2005a; Lu et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2005b), class II mutant IN molecules had variable levels of catalytic activity as assessed by the ability of Vpr-IN proteins to transcomplement a catalytically inactive IN (D116N, Engelman et al., 1995; Engelman and Craigie, 1992) in infected cells (Liu et al., 1997; Fletcher et al., 1997).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: K14A, E96A, Y99A, K103A, V165A, R187A, K188E R199A, K236E, and R269A/R273A IN mutants trans-complemented a catalytically inactive IN at levels similar to the WT.
source: We found that K14A, E96A, Y99A, K103A, V165A, R187A, K188E R199A, K236E, and R269A/R273A IN mutants trans-complemented a catalytically inactive IN at levels similar to the WT, whereas W108R, R228A, and V260E mutants were unable to do so (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: W108R, R228A, and V260E mutants were unable to trans-complement a catalytically inactive IN.
source: We found that K14A, E96A, Y99A, K103A, V165A, R187A, K188E R199A, K236E, and R269A/R273A IN mutants trans-complemented a catalytically inactive IN at levels similar to the WT, whereas W108R, R228A, and V260E mutants were unable to do so (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The inability of W108R, R228A, and V260E mutants to transcomplement implies that they are impaired for integration.
source: The inability of W108R, R228A, and V260E mutants to transcomplement implies that they are impaired for integration, a result in line with previous observations (Lutzke and Plasterk, 1998; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The majority of the class II mutant INs retain structural integrity and at least partial catalytic activity in the presence of a complementing IN protein.
source: These results suggest that the majority of the class II mutant INs retain structural integrity and at least partial catalytic activity in the presence of a complementing IN protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on trans-complementation.

claim: All class II IN mutant viruses contained similar levels of vRNA, ruling out any inadvertent effects of the alterations on RNA packaging.
source: All class II IN mutant viruses contained similar levels of vRNA, ruling out any inadvertent effects of the alterations on RNA packaging (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The catalytically inactive IN D116N bound vRNA at a level that was comparable to the WT.
source: While the catalytically inactive IN D116N bound vRNA at a level that was comparable to the WT, nearly all of the class II IN mutant proteins failed to bind vRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nearly all of the class II IN mutant proteins failed to bind vRNA.
source: While the catalytically inactive IN D116N bound vRNA at a level that was comparable to the WT, nearly all of the class II IN mutant proteins failed to bind vRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The E96A substitution decreased but did not abolish the ability of IN to bind RNA.
source: The E96A substitution, which had a fairly modest effect on virus titers as compared to other IN mutants (Figure 2B), decreased but did not abolish the ability of IN to bind RNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lack of RNA binding ability is a surprisingly common property of a disperse set of class II IN mutants, despite the fact that many of the altered amino acid residues are distally located from the CTD.
source: Thus, lack of RNA binding ability is a surprisingly common property of a disperse set of class II IN mutants, despite the fact that many of the altered amino acid residues are distally located from the CTD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on IN-RNA binding.

claim: IN species that migrated at molecular weights consistent with those of monomers, dimers, trimers, and tetramers were readily distinguished in WT virions.
source: IN species that migrated at molecular weights consistent with those of monomers, dimers, trimers, and tetramers were readily distinguished in WT virions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the majority of the class II mutant particles, IN appeared to exist as monomers as well as higher molecular weight species, representing IN multimers or IN aggregates, with little dimers and no readily detectable tetramers.
source: In the majority of the class II mutant particles, IN appeared to exist as monomers as well as higher molecular weight species, representing IN multimers or IN aggregates, with little dimers and no readily detectable tetramers (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: K34A, E96A, R262A/R263A, and R269A/K273A IN mutants formed dimers and tetramers at similar levels to the WT.
source: In contrast, K34A, E96A, R262A/R263A, and R269A/K273A IN mutants formed dimers and tetramers at similar levels to the WT (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT, K34A, and R262A/R263A INs formed tetramers.
source: In line with the crosslinking studies in virions, WT, K34A, and R262A/R263A INs formed tetramers, while the levels of dimers varied for different mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experimental data.

claim: IN R262A/R263A presented similar levels of tetramers and dimers.
source: For example, while IN R262A/R263A presented similar levels of tetramers and dimers, IN K34A was primarily tetrameric with a minor dimeric species, as evident by the broad right shoulder of the tetrameric SEC peak (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IN K34A was primarily tetrameric with a minor dimeric species.
source: For example, while IN R262A/R263A presented similar levels of tetramers and dimers, IN K34A was primarily tetrameric with a minor dimeric species, as evident by the broad right shoulder of the tetrameric SEC peak (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The majority of other IN mutants almost exclusively formed dimers and monomers with little evidence for tetramer formation.
source: By contrast, the majority of other IN mutants almost exclusively formed dimers and monomers with little evidence for tetramer formation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: WT IN tetramers bound to TAR RNA with high affinity (2.68 ± 0.16 nM).
source: Remarkably, while WT IN tetramers bound to TAR RNA with high affinity (2.68 ± 0.16 nM), neither IN dimers nor monomers showed evidence of binding (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neither IN dimers nor monomers showed evidence of binding to TAR RNA.
source: Remarkably, while WT IN tetramers bound to TAR RNA with high affinity (2.68 ± 0.16 nM), neither IN dimers nor monomers showed evidence of binding (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WT tetramers rather than dimers effectively bridged RNA oligonucleotides in vitro.
source: In line with this, we found that WT tetramers rather than dimers effectively bridged RNA oligonucleotides in vitro (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All class II IN mutants that predominantly formed dimers had reduced affinity for RNA compared to WT IN.
source: All class II IN mutants that predominantly formed dimers (Figure 4B) had reduced affinity for RNA compared to WT IN (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Class II IN mutations that predominantly formed dimers had even more deleterious effects on the ability of IN to bridge the RNA molecules.
source: Furthermore, these mutations had even more deleterious effects on the ability of IN to bridge the RNA molecules (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IN K34A showed a reduced binding affinity for RNA.
source: Although IN K34A and IN R262A/R263A could both form tetramers, IN K34A showed a reduced binding affinity for RNA while IN R262A/R263A did not bind RNA at all (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IN R262A/R263A did not bind RNA at all.
source: Although IN K34A and IN R262A/R263A could both form tetramers, IN K34A showed a reduced binding affinity for RNA while IN R262A/R263A did not bind RNA at all (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by AlphaScreen assay experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: K34A and R262A/R263A residues may be directly involved in IN binding to RNA.
source: Although IN K34A and IN R262A/R263A could both form tetramers, IN K34A showed a reduced binding affinity for RNA while IN R262A/R263A did not bind RNA at all (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that these residues may be directly involved in IN binding to RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these mutants can form tetramers but still cannot bind RNA effectively.

claim: IN tetramerization plays a key role for high-affinity binding to RNA and for RNA bridging.
source: Collectively, these results pointed to a key role of IN tetramerization for high-affinity binding to RNA and more critically for RNA bridging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on IN multimerization and RNA binding.

claim: A defect in proper multimerization underlies the inability of the majority of class II IN mutants to form functional complexes with vRNA.
source: Thus, these findings suggest that a defect in proper multimerization underlies the inability of the majority of class II IN mutants to form functional complexes with vRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on IN multimerization and RNA binding.

claim: Irrespective of how IN-RNA interactions were inhibited, 70–80% of nearly all class II IN mutant particles exhibited an eccentric morphology.
source: Remarkably, irrespective of how IN-RNA interactions were inhibited, 70–80% of nearly all class II IN mutant particles exhibited an eccentric morphology (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The E96A mutant tended to produce less eccentric and more mature particles than the other IN mutants.
source: Of note, the E96A mutant tended to produce less eccentric and more mature particles than the other IN mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM experimental data.

claim: Because IN E96A retained partial binding to vRNA in virions and partial infectivity, this infection-deferred mutant harbors a partial class II phenotype.
source: Because IN E96A retained partial binding to vRNA in virions (Figure 3B) and partial infectivity (Figure 2B), we conclude that this infection-deferred mutant harbors a partial class II phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on RNA binding and infectivity.

claim: WT IN migrated primarily in dense fractions in sucrose gradients.
source: As before (Madison et al., 2017), WT IN migrated primarily in dense fractions, whereas the R269A/K273A mutant migrated bimodally (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The R269A/K273A mutant migrated bimodally in sucrose gradients.
source: As before (Madison et al., 2017), WT IN migrated primarily in dense fractions, whereas the R269A/K273A mutant migrated bimodally (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The majority of IN mutants sedimented similarly to WT IN and settled in the denser gradient fractions.
source: In contrast to our hypothesis, the majority of IN mutants sedimented similarly to WT IN and settled in the denser gradient fractions (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The K34A and R262A/R263A IN mutants, a fraction of which migrated to soluble fractions similar to the R269A/K273A mutant, suggesting their localization outside of the capsid lattice.
source: Exceptions were the K34A and R262A/R263A IN mutants, a fraction of which migrated to soluble fractions similar to the R269A/K273A mutant, suggesting their localization outside of the capsid lattice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data and inferred from the migration pattern.

claim: None of the IN substitutions affected the migration pattern of CA.
source: None of the IN substitutions affected the migration pattern of CA (Figure 7C), which distributed was bimodally between the soluble and dense fractions
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CA distributed bimodally between the soluble and dense fractions.
source: None of the IN substitutions affected the migration pattern of CA (Figure 7C), which distributed was bimodally between the soluble and dense fractions
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The distribution of MA was found in mainly the soluble fractions.
source: nor the distribution of MA (data not shown), which was found in mainly the soluble fractions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data.

claim: The K203A CA mutation caused the loss of CA in the dense fractions compared to WT viruses, indicating that the CA lattice was indeed destabilized.
source: Note that the K203A CA mutation caused the loss of CA in the dense fractions compared to WT viruses, indicating that the CA lattice was indeed destabilized (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The migration of IN in dense fractions over the gradients does not appear to be dependent on its being enclosed in an intact CA lattice.
source: Thus, the migration of IN in dense fractions over the gradients does not appear to be dependent on its being enclosed in an intact CA lattice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with CA K203A mutant.

claim: Lack of RNA packaging and an unstable CA lattice with the Gag-bZIP virus did not affect the migration pattern of IN over the sucrose gradients.
source: Lack of RNA packaging and an unstable CA lattice with the Gag-bZIP virus also did not affect the migration pattern of IN over the sucrose gradients (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), nor did presence of RNAse throughout the fractionation experiment (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by equilibrium density sedimentation experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The migration of IN in dense sucrose gradients is independent of its being enclosed in an intact CA lattice and of its binding to vRNA.
source: The results from these experiments indicate that the migration of IN in dense sucrose gradients is independent of its being enclosed in an intact CA lattice and of its binding to vRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with CA K203A mutant and Gag-bZIP virus.

claim: In cells infected with WT viruses, IN, RT, vRNA, and a fraction of CA comigrated to sucrose fractions 6–8, representing active RTCs.
source: As previously reported (Madison et al., 2017; Kutluay et al., 2013), in cells infected with WT viruses, IN, RT, vRNA, and a fraction of CA comigrated to sucrose fractions 6–8, representing active RTCs (Figure 8B–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation experimental data shown in Figure 8B-E and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In cells infected with class II IN mutant viruses, equivalent levels of CA and RT remained in the denser fractions, whereas IN and vRNA were substantially reduced.
source: Notably, in cells infected with class II IN mutant viruses, equivalent levels of CA (Figure 8B) and RT (Figure 8D) remained in the denser fractions, whereas IN (Figure 8C) and vRNA (Figure 8E) were substantially reduced.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation experimental data shown in Figure 8B-E.

claim: Loss of vRNA and IN from dense fractions, without any corresponding increase in the top fractions containing soluble proteins and RNA, suggest their premature degradation and/or mislocalization in infected cells.
source: Loss of vRNA and IN from dense fractions, without any corresponding increase in the top fractions containing soluble proteins and RNA, suggest their premature degradation and/or mislocalization in infected cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical fractionation experimental data.

claim: In WT-infected cells, cell-associated vRNA had fallen to 60–80% of starting levels two hr post infection.
source: Two hr post infection, cell-associated vRNA had fallen to 60–80% of starting levels (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), likely as the result of some viruses failing to enter or perhaps being degraded after entry.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy-based experimental data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: vRNA levels decreased at a faster rate with the class II IN mutants as compared to WT viruses in MT-4 T cells.
source: In line with the above findings, vRNA levels decreased at a faster rate with the class II IN mutants as compared to WT viruses, with half as much cell-associated vRNA remaining at 2 and 6 hr post-infection for the class II IN mutants (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Q-RT-PCR experimental data in MT-4 T cells shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Treating cells with ammonium chloride to prevent fusion of the VSV-G pseudotyped viruses rescued vRNA loss, and vRNA from WT and mutant viruses were retained at equal levels, indicating that the loss of vRNA is dependent on entry into the target cell.
source: Treating cells with ammonium chloride to prevent fusion of the VSV-G pseudotyped viruses rescued vRNA loss, and vRNA from WT and mutant viruses were retained at equal levels, indicating that the loss of vRNA is dependent on entry into the target cell (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Class II IN substitutions lead to the premature loss of the vRNA genome in human T cells.
source: These findings agree with the previous experiments and demonstrate that class II IN substitutions lead to the premature loss of the vRNA genome also in human T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in MT-4 T cells.

claim: The CTD mediates IN tetramer-tetramer interactions in the higher-order dodecamer IN structure.
source: While not apparent in the tetrameric intasome complex, the CTD mediates IN tetramer-tetramer interactions in the higher-order dodecamer IN structure (Passos et al., 2017) and has also been shown to mediate IN multimerization in vitro (Jenkins et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The CTD has been shown to mediate IN multimerization in vitro.
source: While not apparent in the tetrameric intasome complex, the CTD mediates IN tetramer-tetramer interactions in the higher-order dodecamer IN structure (Passos et al., 2017) and has also been shown to mediate IN multimerization in vitro (Jenkins et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Positively charged residues within the CTD of IN (i.e. K264, K266, K273) directly contact RNA.
source: Based on MS-based footprinting experiments in vitro, we previously found that positively charged residues within the CTD of IN (i.e. K264, K266, K273) directly contact RNA, as was also validated by CLIP experiments (Kessl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: IN-vRNA contacts may extend to nearby basic residues within the CTD, such as R262 and R263.
source: Our findings here suggest that IN-vRNA contacts may extend to nearby basic residues within the CTD, such as R262 and R263
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that R262A/R263A mutants cannot bind RNA despite forming tetramers.

claim: IN-vRNA contacts may extend to K34 within the IN NTD.
source: and perhaps more surprisingly, K34 within the IN NTD, as alterations of these residues did not prevent IN tetramerization (Figure 4A–B) but completely abolished IN-vRNA binding in virions (Figure 3B) and reduced RNA-binding in vitro (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that K34A mutant cannot bind RNA despite forming tetramers.

claim: There may be a second RNA-binding site in the IN NTD.
source: This raises the possibility of a second RNA-binding site in the IN NTD.
evidence: This is speculated based on the finding that K34A affects RNA binding without affecting tetramerization.

claim: The bimodal distribution of IN in the experimental setting was only seen with IN mutants that directly inhibited IN binding to vRNA.
source: It is intriguing that the bimodal distribution of IN in this experimental setting was only seen with IN mutants that directly inhibited IN binding to vRNA.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Improperly multimerized IN is retained within the CA lattice or in association with it.
source: A possible explanation for these observations is that improperly multimerized IN is retained within the CA lattice or in association with it.
evidence: This is a possible explanation proposed for the experimental observations.

claim: Class II IN mutants that may localize outside of the CA lattice form dense aggregates and as a result migrate similar to WT IN.
source: Alternatively, class II IN mutants that may localize outside of the CA lattice form dense aggregates and as a result migrate similar to WT IN.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation proposed for the experimental observations.

claim: Select class II IN mutants migrate similar to WT IN upon CA destabilization but are rapidly lost in infected cells.
source: The fact that select class II IN mutants migrate similar to WT IN upon CA destabilization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) but are rapidly lost in infected cells (Figure 8C), strongly suggests the latter possibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The protection afforded by the CA lattice matters the most for vRNP stability.
source: It seems evident that the protection afforded by the CA lattice matters the most for vRNP stability, though we cannot rule out that IN binding to vRNA may in and of itself stabilize both the genome and IN.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing premature loss of vRNA and IN in infected cells.

claim: The AU-rich nucleotide content of HIV-1 may destabilize its RNA.
source: Alternatively, the AU-rich nucleotide content of HIV-1 may destabilize its RNA (Maldarelli et al., 1991; Schwartz et al., 1992a; Schwartz et al., 1992b), similar to several cellular mRNAs that encode for cytokines and growth factors (Wu and Brewer, 2012).
evidence: This is a possible explanation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNA nicking and deadenylation in virions by virion-associated enzymes may predispose retroviral genomes to degradation when they are prematurely exposed to the cytosolic milieu.
source: Finally, RNA nicking and deadenylation in virions by virion-associated enzymes (Gorelick et al., 1999; Miyazaki et al., 2010; Sakuragi et al., 2001) may predispose retroviral genomes to degradation when they are prematurely exposed to the cytosolic milieu.
evidence: This is a possible explanation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proteasome inhibition does not rescue vRNA or IN in target cells infected with a class II IN mutant.
source: While cytosolic IN undergoes proteasomal degradation when expressed alone in cells (Mulder and Muesing, 2000; Ali et al., 2019; Llano et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2011; Devroe et al., 2003), we have found previously that proteasome inhibition does not rescue vRNA or IN in target cells infected with a class II IN mutant (Madison et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutations within the C-terminus of murine leukemia virus (MLV) IN can cause defects in reverse transcription.
source: Interestingly, mutations within the C-terminus of murine leukemia virus (MLV) IN can similarly cause defects in reverse transcription (Steinrigl et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2001), raising the possibility of a conserved role for IN in particle maturation and reverse transcription across retroviruses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a possibility of a conserved role for IN in particle maturation and reverse transcription across retroviruses.
source: Interestingly, mutations within the C-terminus of murine leukemia virus (MLV) IN can similarly cause defects in reverse transcription (Steinrigl et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2001), raising the possibility of a conserved role for IN in particle maturation and reverse transcription across retroviruses.
evidence: This is speculated based on observations in MLV.

claim: Virion morphogenesis is necessary to prevent the premature loss of vRNA and IN early in the HIV-1 lifecycle.
source: In conclusion, we have identified IN-vRNA binding as the underlying factor for the role of IN in virion morphogenesis and show that virion morphogenesis is necessary to prevent the premature loss of vRNA and IN early in the HIV-1 lifecycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: IN-vRNA interaction can be inhibited in multiple ways – by directly altering residues in the IN CTD or by altering IN multimerization in virions.
source: The finding that IN-vRNA interaction can be inhibited in multiple ways – by directly altering residues in the IN CTD or by altering IN multimerization in virions – can help guide the design of future anti-retroviral compounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.
